pageTwo.name: Local Rules
pageTwo.headline: CUT IT AND IT GROWS BACK.
pageTwo.dek: An interactive essay on cellular automata: six simulations, all computed on your own GPU, from Conway’s Game of Life to a neural network that was never told what shape to become.
story: Every simulation in this essay runs on one idea: each cell on the grid looks only at its immediate neighbours, applies a single rule, and knows nothing about the picture it belongs to. Nobody tells the grid what to draw. The structure that appears — gliders, spots, stripes, whole organisms — is what falls out of that rule, applied everywhere at once.

There are six of them, ordered by how alive they get: Conway’s Game of Life, the wider rule space around it, Larger than Life, Lenia, reaction–diffusion, and finally a neural cellular automaton. All six are computed on the reader’s own graphics card through WebGPU compute shaders — nothing here is a recorded video. Conway sustains 5.8 billion cell updates per second on a 2048×2048 grid. Lenia’s much larger neighbourhood is convolved with an FFT instead, which overtakes direct convolution past a radius of about nine and runs roughly 2.4× faster at the radius actually used.

The last one was never programmed. It is a network of 8,336 numbers — 33 kilobytes, smaller than a screenshot of its own output — trained offline in PyTorch until a single lit pixel reliably grows into one specific creature. Drag the cursor through it and it does not restore a saved copy, because it doesn’t have one. Each surviving cell renegotiates with its neighbours, and the shape closes over the wound.

Every figure quoted above was measured on real hardware rather than estimated, and where a measurement was not taken the page prints a dash instead of a guess — a policy this newspaper warmly recommends to its competitors. —
